p1.title: Passage 1
paras: India is unusual in giving official recognition to several systems of medicine. Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy are grouped under AYUSH and supported by a separate ministry, research councils and a network of dispensaries. Supporters argue that these systems are affordable, culturally familiar and well suited to chronic and lifestyle disorders, where long-term care matters more than dramatic intervention. Integrating AYUSH practitioners into primary health centres could also ease the shortage of doctors in rural areas. Critics, however, point out that the evidence base for many traditional remedies remains thin, and that patients may delay effective treatment for serious illness. The challenge, then, is not to choose one system over another but to build an integrated framework in which each system is used where it works best, supported by rigorous research, clear referral pathways and honest communication with patients.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: Within living memory, a villager on a clear night could see the pale band of the Milky Way stretching from horizon to horizon. For most city-dwellers today it is invisible, washed out by the glow of streetlights, advertising hoardings and illuminated buildings. Light pollution is easily dismissed as an aesthetic loss of concern only to astronomers, but its effects reach further. Many creatures navigate, feed and breed by the cycle of light and darkness. Hatchling sea turtles, which crawl towards the brightest horizon, are lured inland by beachfront lights instead of towards the sea; migrating birds collide with lit towers; nocturnal insects circle lamps until they are exhausted, depriving the animals that feed on them. Human beings are not exempt, for exposure to bright light at night disturbs the hormonal rhythms that govern sleep.

Unlike many environmental problems, this one is unusually easy to reverse. Darkness returns the moment a lamp is switched off or shielded. Fixtures that direct light downwards onto the road rather than sideways into the sky, warmer and dimmer bulbs, and timers that switch off decorative lighting after midnight can greatly reduce the glow without compromising safety. Such measures also save electricity. What is lacking is not technology but recognition that the night, too, is a resource worth conserving.

questions.q: The passage primarily presents AYUSH systems as
opts: officially recognised systems with both strengths and limitations
questions.why: Main idea: balanced; the author weighs supporters and critics. Passage: GPSC-style practice passage (2026 pattern).

questions.q: Which system is NOT named in the passage as part of AYUSH?
questions.why: NOT question: acupuncture is not listed. Passage: GPSC-style practice passage (2026 pattern).

questions.q: According to supporters, AYUSH systems are especially suited to
questions.why: Detail: the third sentence. Passage: GPSC-style practice passage (2026 pattern).

opts: There are too many AYUSH doctors
The evidence for many remedies is thin and patients may delay effective treatment
questions.why: Detail: the fifth sentence. Passage: GPSC-style practice passage (2026 pattern).

an integrated framework, backed by research and referral, is needed

questions.q: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
opts: New technology must be invented before light pollution can be reduced.
Light pollution matters only to astronomers.
Cities need brighter lighting to ensure public safety.
Light pollution harms wildlife and people, and can be easily remedied once darkness is valued.
questions.why: Main idea: its 'effects reach further' than astronomy, and 'What is lacking is not technology but recognition that the night, too, is a resource'.

questions.q: According to the passage, what happens to hatchling sea turtles near lit beaches?
opts: They are lured inland instead of moving towards the sea.
questions.why: Detail: they 'are lured inland by beachfront lights instead of towards the sea'.

questions.q: The author calls light pollution 'unusually easy to reverse' chiefly because:
opts: unlike many pollutants, artificial light leaves no lasting residue once it is removed.
new bulbs are cheaper than old ones.
most cities have already banned decorative lighting.
animals quickly adapt to bright light.
questions.why: Inference: 'Darkness returns the moment a lamp is switched off or shielded', in contrast to 'many environmental problems' whose effects persist.

questions.q: The tone of the final sentence of the passage is:
opts: despairing about the future of the night sky.
persuasive, urging a change in how the night is regarded.
questions.why: Tone: the author urges 'recognition that the night, too, is a resource worth conserving'.

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'exempt' means:
opts: free from an effect that applies to others
questions.why: Vocabulary: 'Human beings are not exempt' means they too suffer the effects that harm turtles, birds and insects.
